We introduced Controlled Style Decomposition (CSD), a black-box framework that reveals the Likert Blindspot---systematic measurement attenuation in Likert scoring---across three judges, three benchmarks, and three style axes.
The Blindspot is not merely a statistical power gap: at moderate bias levels (BT 63--67\%), Likert compresses effect sizes to zero even at $n = 355$; at stronger effects, it attenuates by over 60\%.
Seven statistical methods confirm this is structural, not an artifact of any particular test.

Verbosity provides the cleanest evidence: both judges show 76--77\% pairwise preference for verbose responses with confound-free identification (Originality n.s.), yet Likert detects nothing.
GEE conditional decomposition reveals that formality and register exhibit conditional style effects alongside originality confounds, motivating per-axis analysis over aggregate style metrics.

For the evaluation community, the practical implication is clear: style bias audits should adopt pairwise comparison, especially at the moderate effect sizes typical of real-world evaluation ($n < 500$).
Existing Likert-based null findings may reflect measurement insensitivity rather than genuine absence of bias.
Future work should incorporate human evaluation of rewriting quality, broader benchmark and axis coverage, and stronger causal identification through randomized rather than observational designs.
